reels.title: The Income Statement
reels.content: Lists revenue, expenses, and taxes over a period of time (quarter/year).
key_points: Revenue - COGS = Gross Profit
Gross Profit - OpEx - D&A = Operating Income
Operating Income +/- Other = Pre-Tax Income
Pre-Tax Income - Taxes = Net Income (bottom line)
reels.golden_rule: To appear on the IS: must affect taxes AND correspond to the period shown.
reels.pro_tip: Never appears: CapEx, Dividends, Debt Principal, Share Repurchases

reels.title: The Balance Sheet
reels.content: Shows Assets and how they were funded (Liabilities + Equity) at a point in time.
key_points: Assets = Liabilities + Equity (ALWAYS)
Current = under 1 year | Long-Term = over 1 year
Assets: Cash, AR, Inventory, PP&E, Goodwill
Liabilities: AP, Debt, Deferred Revenue
Equity: Common Stock, Retained Earnings, Treasury Stock
reels.golden_rule: Assets must ALWAYS equal Liabilities + Equity. No exceptions.
reels.pro_tip: Think of YOUR balance sheet: house + savings = mortgage + saved earnings

reels.title: The Cash Flow Statement
reels.content: Tracks actual cash changes over a period. Exists because the IS has non-cash items.
key_points: CFO: Net Income + non-cash adjustments + WC changes
CFI: CapEx, acquisitions, investment purchases/sales
CFF: Debt issued/repaid, dividends, share buybacks
Beginning Cash + Total Changes = Ending Cash
reels.golden_rule: If it was on the IS and is real cash, it does NOT reappear here.
reels.pro_tip: Depreciation is added back in CFO because it reduced Net Income but is not real cash.

reels.title: Linking the 3 Statements
reels.content: The 3 financial statements are interconnected in a specific flow.
key_points: 1. Net Income flows from IS to top of CFS
2. CFS adjusts for non-cash items and working capital
3. Net change in cash updates Cash on BS
4. Retained Earnings on BS += Net Income - Dividends
5. BS must STILL balance after all changes
reels.golden_rule: Always follow: Income Statement -> Cash Flow Statement -> Balance Sheet.
reels.pro_tip: This is THE most common interview question. Practice it until automatic.

reels.title: How Changes Flow Through
reels.content: When something changes, it ripples through all 3 statements.
key_points: Example: Depreciation goes UP by $10 (40% tax rate)
IS: Pre-Tax Income falls $10, Net Income falls $6
CFS: Net Income -$6, add back D&A +$10 = Cash +$4
BS: Cash +$4, PP&E -$10 = Assets -$6
BS: Retained Earnings -$6 = L+E -$6. BALANCED.
reels.golden_rule: Always trace: IS impact -> tax effect -> CFS adjustments -> BS balance check.
reels.pro_tip: Tax rate matters! $10 expense only reduces cash by $6 if tax rate is 40%.

reels.title: What is a DCF?
reels.content: Values a company based on its future cash flows, discounted to present value.
key_points: 1. Project Free Cash Flow for 5-10 years
2. Calculate Terminal Value (far-future value)
3. Discount both back to today using WACC
4. Sum of both = Enterprise Value
5. Enterprise Value - Net Debt = Equity Value
reels.golden_rule: A company is worth the present value of ALL its future cash flows.
reels.pro_tip: Terminal Value is usually 50-80% of total value. If >85%, check your assumptions.

reels.title: Revenue to Free Cash Flow
reels.content: How to calculate Unlevered Free Cash Flow (UFCF) step by step.
key_points: Revenue - COGS - OpEx = EBIT
EBIT x (1 - Tax Rate) = NOPAT
+ Depreciation & Amortization
- Changes in Working Capital
- Capital Expenditures
= Unlevered Free Cash Flow
reels.golden_rule: UFCF excludes interest/debt effects. Shows cash available to ALL investors.
reels.pro_tip: Levered FCF subtracts interest and mandatory debt repayments (for equity holders only).

reels.title: WACC & Discount Rate
reels.content: Weighted Average Cost of Capital - the rate to discount future cash flows.
key_points: WACC = %Equity x Cost of Equity + %Debt x Cost of Debt x (1-Tax)
Cost of Equity = Risk-Free Rate + Beta x Equity Risk Premium
Risk-Free Rate = 10-year government bond yield
Beta measures stock volatility vs. the market
Higher WACC = lower present value = lower valuation
reels.golden_rule: WACC represents the blended required return for ALL investors (debt + equity).
reels.pro_tip: Typical WACC ranges: 8-12% for most companies. Lower for stable, higher for risky.

reels.title: Terminal Value
reels.content: Represents the company's value BEYOND the projection period.
key_points: Gordon Growth: FCF x (1+g) / (WACC - g)
Multiples Method: Final Year EBITDA x Exit Multiple
Growth rate (g) should be <= GDP growth (2-3%)
Must discount Terminal Value back to present
Usually 50-80% of total Enterprise Value
reels.golden_rule: Long-term growth can NEVER exceed GDP growth. No company grows forever.
reels.pro_tip: Multiples Method is more common in banking. Gordon Growth is more academic.

reels.title: Equity Value vs Enterprise Value
reels.content: Two ways to measure what a company is worth - for different audiences.
key_points: Equity Value = Share Price x Diluted Shares
Enterprise Value = Equity Value + Debt + Pref + MI - Cash
Equity Value = value to SHAREHOLDERS only
Enterprise Value = value to ALL investors
EV is capital-structure neutral (better for comparisons)
reels.golden_rule: Match metrics: EV with EBIT/EBITDA/Revenue. Equity Value with Net Income/EPS.
reels.pro_tip: When the news says 'a $10B company', they usually mean Equity Value.

reels.title: Why Enterprise Value Matters
reels.content: EV tells you what you'd REALLY pay to acquire a company.
key_points: Buying a company = buying its equity + assuming its debt
But you also get its cash (offsets the price)
EV = what an acquirer truly pays, net of cash received
Preferred Stock and Minority Interest also add to cost
That's why EV = Equity + Debt + Pref + MI - Cash
reels.golden_rule: Think of buying a house: price (equity) + mortgage (debt) - cash in safe = true cost.
reels.pro_tip: Companies with lots of cash have EV < Equity Value. Heavily indebted: EV >> Equity Value.

reels.title: How an LBO Works
reels.content: A PE firm buys a company using mostly debt, improves it, and sells for profit.
key_points: PE firm puts in 30-40% equity, 60-70% debt
Company's cash flow pays down the debt over 3-7 years
PE firm sells at exit: debt repaid, remainder = profit
Returns: IRR target 20%+, MOIC target 2-3x
Key levers: growth, margins, debt paydown, multiple expansion
reels.golden_rule: An LBO works when the company generates enough cash flow to service the debt.
reels.pro_tip: Think: buy a house with 30% down, rent it out, tenant pays mortgage, sell in 5 years.

reels.title: LBO Returns: The 4 Levers
reels.content: Four ways a PE firm increases returns in an LBO.
key_points: 1. Revenue Growth: grow the top line organically or via acquisitions
2. Margin Expansion: cut costs, improve efficiency
3. Debt Paydown: use cash flow to reduce debt (more equity at exit)
4. Multiple Expansion: sell at a higher EV/EBITDA than you bought
Debt paydown is the most reliable lever
reels.golden_rule: Even with 0% growth, debt paydown alone can generate strong returns.
reels.pro_tip: Multiple expansion is the least controllable. Never assume it in a base case.

reels.title: Accretion / Dilution
reels.content: The key M&A question: does the deal increase or decrease the buyer's EPS?
key_points: Accretive = buyer's EPS goes UP after the deal
Dilutive = buyer's EPS goes DOWN after the deal
Cash deal: compare target's yield vs. lost interest (after tax)
Stock deal: compare P/E ratios
If buyer P/E > target P/E = likely accretive (stock deal)
reels.golden_rule: In a stock deal, the company with the HIGHER P/E ratio wins.
reels.pro_tip: Most large deals are dilutive in Year 1 but accretive by Year 2-3 (synergies kick in).

reels.title: Goodwill & Purchase Price
reels.content: When you buy a company, you almost always pay MORE than its book value.
key_points: Purchase Price - Fair Value of Net Assets = Goodwill
Net Assets = Assets - Liabilities (at fair value, not book)
Goodwill sits on the BS as a Long-Term Asset
Goodwill is NOT amortized (tested annually for impairment)
If you pay LESS than fair value = Negative Goodwill (rare)
reels.golden_rule: Goodwill represents the premium paid for brand, talent, synergies, and market position.
reels.pro_tip: Goodwill impairment is a big red flag: it means the acquisition destroyed value.

reels.title: The Valuation Toolkit
reels.content: Three main methods to value a company, each with different strengths.
key_points: 1. Public Comps: multiples of similar public companies
2. Precedent Transactions: multiples from similar M&A deals
3. DCF: intrinsic value based on projected cash flows
Precedents > Comps (includes control premium of 20-40%)
Always present a valuation RANGE, not a single number
reels.golden_rule: Use a 'football field' chart showing ranges from each method to triangulate fair value.
reels.pro_tip: If all 3 methods agree on a range, you have high conviction. If they diverge, dig deeper.

reels.title: Key Multiples to Know
reels.content: The most commonly used valuation multiples in investment banking.
key_points: EV/Revenue: high-growth, pre-profit companies (SaaS: 5-15x)
EV/EBITDA: most common enterprise multiple (6-12x typical)
EV/EBIT: like EBITDA but captures D&A differences
P/E: most common equity multiple (15-25x typical)
P/BV (Price/Book): for banks and financial institutions
reels.golden_rule: NEVER divide Equity Value by an enterprise metric (or vice versa). They must match.
reels.pro_tip: Higher growth = higher multiple. Compare multiples WITHIN the same industry only.
